Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time.

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI . We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.
Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.
Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura , down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.
A Sprawling Exhibition of Latin American Art and Fashion Is Coming to NYC
Twenty artists and designers across the Americas will be featured in "Malvestir" at MoMA PS1 this spring, probing the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.

Patricia Belli, Troy Montes Michie, Willy Chavarria, and Camila Falquéz are among the 20 artists and designers who will be featured in Malvestir , MoMA PS1's upcoming exhibition on the visual lexicon of Latin American fashion, opening in April 2027.

A portmanteau of the Spanish words mal (poorly) and vestir (to dress), Malvestir features creatives across the Americas who probe the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress. Western appropriations of Indigenous crafts, exorbitant textile waste, and the fetishization of Latin American styles are just some of the key concerns that will be interrogated in the exhibition.

Curated by MoMA PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González, Malvestir will include a range of artists, from New York City designers to textile artists reinvigorating intergenerational weaving traditions.

Several designers are striving to reclaim styles and symbols co-opted by mainstream Western markets. Known for his oversized proportions and street-style designs emblematic of the Mexican-American fashion tradition, New York designer Willy Chavarria is showing Safe From Home (2024), a film that expanded upon themes of love and the right to safety explored in his Autumn/Winter 2024 collection. Malvestir will also include the work of designer Carla Fernández, who nurtures collaborations with local artisans in Mexico to preserve Indigenous motifs against corporate reproduction and profiteering.

Works from multimedia artists who use photography, drawing, painting, sculpture, and textiles to preserve intergenerational customs will also be on view. New Mexico-based artist Josh Tafoya revitalizes his family’s weaving tradition through the centuries-long practice of Rio Grande loom weaving. David Ramirez Cotón pays homage to Guatemalan fashion with a series of hyperrealistic acrylic-on-canvas paintings cut to resemble articles of clothing hanging from a rack in a second-hand shop.

The exhibition comes at a time when Latin American communities are facing regressive crackdowns from multiple parties — the federal government, exploitative corporations, and immigration enforcement. Yet it has also prompted many to recognize the importance of Latinx artists through displaying the full range and power of their respective cultures, as mainstream appropriation and demands for assimilation reach new, threatening extremes.

In an opinion for Hyperallergic this month, Arlene Dávila, a professor of anthropology and American Studies at New York University, positioned the current political climate as a rallying cry for Latinx visionaries.

Within her essay, she referenced Chavarria and Raul Lopez (founder of LUAR), two of the artists whose work will appear in Malvestir , underscoring how they " frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways. "

" Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins," Dávila wrote. "While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary."
In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism
An intergenerational group of artists confronts technology as both a pathogen and a cure for today’s cultural ailments in the husk of an office at 260 Madison.

A few hours before 260 Madison opened on September 24, I trekked to its namesake address in Midtown to meet the curators. A security guard directed me to the 14th floor of the 1950s office building, where drop ceilings, an exposed HVAC system, and two people I assumed were the exhibition organizers dressed in corporate drag greeted me. They quickly clarified they were not ; they were from AmTrustRE, the real estate company that offered the derelict 23,000-square-foot office space to the artists for free while preparing it — and three other unoccupied floors — for their next corporate tenants.

The three artists-turned-curators, Shaina Tabak, Dayana Matasheva, and Edson Niebla Rodríguez (the latter two of whom make up the duo DemonLovers Inc.), organized 260 Madison as an intergenerational, “inter-everything” show with work by over 50 artists, including self-taught and non-traditionally educated practitioners. On view through this Sunday, November 22, the show arrives just as the Whitney Museum of American Art opens artport: A History of Internet Art , signaling a new wave of institutional recognition for internet-grown art. With 260 Madison artists Maya Man, Rachel Rossin, and Eva and Franco Mattes among those included in the Whitney’s 25th-anniversary exhibition for its net art commissioning platform, the Midtown show feels especially urgent, if only because it takes place at the precipice of a paradigmatic shift within the art world.

Upon entering the first room on the left, I was immediately met with artist Jon Kessler’s towering nine-foot-tall sculpture, in which four plastic male dolls in Adidas tracksuits dangled from a weighted contraption somewhere between a carnival ride and a torture device. Titled “It Takes a Global Village Idiot” (2018) after philosopher Marshall McLuhan’s early ’60s theory that information-age technology “recreates the world in the image of a global village,” the sculpture forces viewers to confront the fact that the quick fixes of amusement proffered by technology rely on the same methods of data extraction that undergird systemic violence. It’s an unsettling introduction to a show where, even in its more humorous, delusionally conspiratorial, or enchanting moments, discomfort is always in the periphery.

“We don’t want to make a show or art that tries to be some form of escapism,” Rogríguez told Hyperallergic during an interview the week after the opening. “It’s like the [Werner Herzog] quote, ‘The poet must not avert his eyes.’ If some art in the show seems depressing, it’s because we live in what seems a depressing time.”

Rodríguez and Matasheva, who are also a couple, began making work together seven years ago while studying film in Montreal. Their video-art duo is named after Olivier Assayas’s 2002 film Demonlover , where multiple global corporations compete for a new immersive Japanese hentai company through extreme methods of espionage, exploitation, and blackmail.

“DemonLovers is about the libidinal economy and how algorithms are weaponizing our very basic instincts and desires,” Matasheva told Hyperallergic , echoing Rodríguez’s interest in what he calls “financial Freud,” or the psychoanalytic dimension of digital capital flows.

Both DemonLovers’s own two works in the show and those they curated certainly don’t shy away from the degradation associated with extractive economies, be it of the self, physical infrastructure, or the proverbial global village. Nearby Kessler’s work, Theresa Tomi Faison’s “The Long Tail” (2026) climbs up one of the floor’s load-bearing columns. Across the curved sculpture’s six screens, images of memes, forum screenshots, and phrases ruminating on contemporary capital flow all accumulate and dissolve downstream. The river of digital spam ends at the viewer’s feet, inculcating the audience, but also the space itself, which the curators characterize as shaped by "junkspace” — architect Rem Koolhaas's term for fallout that “remains after modernization has run its course.”

This year’s historic actions demonstrated that Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine will not be ignored — and that the power of boycott has never been greater.
This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed , the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself.

Many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

The massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years ). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions.

The Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “ anywhere or not at all ” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?
A how-to guide on all things inventory, planning, appraisals, conservation, and more.

Much has been written about the “ Great Wealth Transfer ,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing important work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

Ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass quickly to heirs, and also provides great privacy.

When it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, said, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective , can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

Stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt , which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”

When I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

An appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish new cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History
In a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church, a group of women is sewing the legacies of enslaved people into their quilts.

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project . The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

“A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross ; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she says. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”

The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.

After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic .
“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center , which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara ’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center , where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner ’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery , 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake . The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.
‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists

In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising .

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson —the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.
For quilter Rosy Petri , Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery .

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network ( WCQN ), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier ’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp ’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix— in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak ’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”
We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release , Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers .

Her portraits, often accompanied by animals, carry a dreamlike quality, although there is nothing entirely removed from reality about them. A dream can vividly express a narrative that can bleed into your reality and make you feel that what you experience is even more than real.

Reality is full of wonder and mystery in itself, and if we slow down to take in all the aspects of life and decay that construct this circle of life that we are all embarked upon, we’ll experience a profound appreciation for the art of being, as well as the art of creation.

Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from.

If you love your bourbon as much as I do, then you'll know every bottle of Maker's Mark is still dipped in red wax by hand. It's a slow and messy process any creative can appreciate, especially in a year when Cambridge Dictionary named 'human' its word of 2026.

So it makes sense that the brand's new global identity would go down the same route. Turner Duckworth London has taken stalks of soft red winter wheat, rings of American oak and plants native to Star Hill Farm, the distillery's home in Loretto, Kentucky, and dipped and pressed each one into that same red wax. What came out of that is a set of fresh marks that sit at the heart of the brand. There's also an updated colour palette, new photography and custom typography that pays homage to the brand's family roots.

Sound familiar? That's because Turner Duckworth has been here before. We covered its first Maker's Mark identity in 2021 , when the agency built a system around a graphic version of the famous drip. Five years later, the drawing has made way for the real thing. Why illustrate wax when you've got access to vats of it?

The typography has its own story, too. It's inspired by the handwriting of Margie Samuels, who founded Maker's Mark with her husband, Bill Samuels Sr, and who came up with the bottle, label and wax in the first place. It is Margie's wit that the brand has always traded on. Well, I never.

Now for a little history lesson. Bill famously burned the family's 170-year-old recipe to start afresh and come up with a more balanced bourbon. The couple chose Loretto for its proximity to water and grain growers. And Margie decided that every bottle must be hand-dipped – a strategy that literally made its mark. Maker's Mark calls this streak 'Perfectly Unreasonable', the name of its brand platform, and the new identity is designed to carry this idea consistently worldwide, in what the brand describes as a "modern, more minimal way".

"In a world increasingly driven by speed and automation, we still believe some things are worth making slowly, by hand," says Chloe Lloyd-Jones, vice president of global brand marketing, Maker's Mark. "We returned to Star Hill Farm, working with natural materials from the land and our signature red wax to create a visual identity that reflects the 'Perfectly Unreasonable' spirit behind our bourbon. The result gives us a powerful way to tell our story around the world, while creating experiences that feel personal and relevant in each market."

"My grandparents weren't thinking about 'branding' when they created Maker's Mark. They cared about a hand-made process in service to flavour and design that honours that vision," adds Rob Samuels, eighth-generation whisky maker and managing director. "That deeply personal approach created some of the most recognisable symbols in bourbon. This new and exceptional work brings that same intention forward, honouring what they created and ensuring Maker's Mark feels as personal and distinctive today as it did from the start."

The identity was launched on 17 November and is rolling out across digital, social, advertising and retail, as well as events and experiences. Parts of it have already appeared at events in the US and China and in out-of-home campaigns in Australia and the UK, with more markets to follow throughout 2027.

So why didn't they start from scratch? One would assume the importance of heritage, certainly. By Insomnia's own account, it created the warm cookie delivery category, and &Walsh set out to recommit to that rather than reinvent it. So whilst everyone else is chasing trends, the new strategy focuses on a single promise: 'Always Warm'. Gosh, my mouth is watering just thinking about it.

That brand promise suits Insomnia's purpose – turning up at your door at any unreasonable hour with something straight from the oven. It's why the agency didn't overcomplicate things or try and be clever. When you look at this refreshed logo, you get that instant promise. It's confident without trying too hard.

Around the moon is a system built on the hours Insomnia operates. There's a nice late-night purple palette (Premier Inn, anyone?), along with a run of cookie-dough browns. Typography by Julio Zukerman is rounded and chunky. Illustration is also by Julio and Simran Meshram. And there's a refreshed tone of voice throughout.

Then there's Insomnia's menu, which rotates constantly. And every limited-time offer is another opportunity for the brand to show off its new look. To keep it all feeling like one brand, &Walsh designed a tiered system: most launches share the same warm, appetising photography and art direction, while a select few campaigns get a more graphic approach.

What's really interesting is the sheer volume of the work. Over six months, &Walsh produced more than five photography and video shoots to cover 12 campaigns, from the core range of cookies to seasonal specials. OK, now I want to know about seasonal specials. Photography was by Henry Hargreaves, while Charlotte Omnes and Daniella Khan handled food styling. Motion design is by Pedro Magalhães, Igor Fajardo and Marco Del Pra, and moving elements can be seen across the refresh. It looks so good you can almost see the heat coming off the freshly baked cookies.

"Every decision in this rebrand, the photo moon cookie, the photography, the rounded type, the colours, was built toward the same feeling: warm, late night and confident," says Carolina Vazquez, art director at &Walsh. "The goal was to make the brand feel fresh without losing what's always made it Insomnia."
Given how much I'll be playing GTA 6 over the coming weeks, I reckon I could be persuaded to enjoy a late-night cookie.

Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question.

This time last year, many creatives were rushing to adopt AI tools, but nervously. Twelve months later, things have changed a lot. That's according to Beyond the Hype: The State of AI in Creative Work , the second annual report from Envato , the creative asset and AI toolkit owned by Shutterstock.

Based on a survey of 1,033 creatives across 103 countries and territories, the report reveals what creatives are actually doing with AI. And two big things immediately grabbed my attention. Firstly, more than half of AI users have used it on key client work without telling their client. And secondly, while AI may save you time, most creatives aren't seeing that turn into actual money.
To unpack these findings and more, I spoke to Hichame Assi, president of Shutterstock, which includes Envato.

Envato first ran the survey in 2025, and Hichame says the reason was simple. The public conversation about AI didn't match what he was seeing from the working creatives who use Envato. "At face value, the narrative was all hype or doom," he recalls. "Yet in our community, creatives were quietly working AI into client jobs." So last year, Envato asked creatives how they were using it.

One finding from that first survey stayed with Hichame in particular. "Almost half were using AI every day, but only about a third felt really prepared for it. That gap felt worth keeping an eye on, so we came back to see what had changed."
So what has changed in the last 12 months? Well, quite a lot actually. For a start, today 87% of creatives use AI at work at least occasionally, and 58% use it every day.

"AI is now part of the daily routine for most creatives," says Hichame. "Daily use rose from 49% to 58%, and agentic tools, which we didn't even ask about last year, are now used regularly by more than a third of AI users. At the same time, active avoidance has grown from 3% to 8%, so not everyone is on board yet."
But while most creatives are using AI to help them in their work, that doesn't mean that AI is doing their work, at least not all of it.

The survey split people's creative work into six stages, from research and admin to editing. At five of the six stages, "directing [AI] closely" was the most common approach. The percentage of creatives who let AI work "with little input" never went above 11%, and at some stages, it dropped to 4%. As for generating assets, only 7% took a hands-off approach.
For Hichame, the biggest surprise in this year's data concerned the skill that, only a year ago, everyone seemed to agree was essential: prompting.

"Last year, our respondents named prompting as a skills gap and predicted 'prompt engineer' as a new job," he recalls. "This year, though, creatives ranked it last of eight factors, at 19%." Taste and judgement came first, at 53%. Craft came second, at 49%, followed by the strength of the idea, at 39%.

So what's going on? Perhaps this is just a sign that models have got much better at understanding natural language and visual references. Consequently, the time when precise prompts were all-important is long gone.

"The tools are going to keep getting easier and more accessible, so knowing how to use them won't be what sets creatives apart," says Jessica Walsh, founder of New York studio &Walsh and one of the experts interviewed for the report. What will, in her view, is "being able to recognise great work when you see it [which is] not something you can prompt, or learn overnight."

One thing that surprised me personally is that nearly six in 10 creatives who work in teams say they have no written AI policy. Even in organisations of 250 or more people, four in 10 say they've been given nothing in writing. As Hichame puts it: "The tools moved fast, and the rules didn't. Most are working it out as they go." Which brings us to a thorny question: should creatives disclose whether they've used AI in their work?

The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images.

Julie Legrand's portfolio is full of things you've seen a thousand times and probably never stopped to really look at, let alone draw them. There's a moka pot drawn in a wobbly black line, a large-scale sunshine-yellow coffee pot on chocolatey brown, a hand holding a shell among pale blue crabs and whelks, and roses in all sorts of guises, from a yellow bloom with 'ROSA' scrawled underneath in her own lettering to a tomato-red one floating on cobalt blue. A few simple shapes, a handful of colours and the odd paper dot from a hole punch are all it takes to make a kitchen staple feel like a star. And it's all so cheerful and homely that we want to put the kettle on, and maybe pin a few of these to the fridge.

The illustrator and screen printer comes from the south of France. "I grew up in the mountains of the Hérault hinterland," she says, before studying illustration in Épinal, eastern France, and later printmaking in Galicia, Spain. Those roots led her to work with traditional techniques, and are perhaps a key reason why rural life and seaside imagery turn up again and again in her work.

When asked where she finds inspiration, she says: "Primarily from everyday life: objects I find in my kitchen or my studio." That's the sort of stuff we all have lying around at home. Her themes are always "rooted in the intimate and the mundane," and she adds: "I try to convey the memories and poetry associated with them." Since moving to Sète, the sea has crept into her work, including its plant life, mineral forms and inhabitants. "I like to interpret the landscape through the elements and forms that compose it, rather than by representing the landscape itself."

Once she has her inspiration in check, she moves on to her process. "I exhaust forms," she explains, "meaning I choose an object or subject and explore its variations, sometimes over the course of months." That explains why a coffee pot and rose each show up in so many guises. She starts with photos, sketches, and drawings she's happy with, then works in collage or with pens, pencils, rulers, and lettering templates, before digitising and editing. The handcrafted feel matters enormously to her, so the paper textures from her collages and the marks and smudges on her drawings all make it through. "Cleaning up a scan is the opposite of my approach," she says – and we're glad.

Recently, Julie created a pair of collages for the Slow Down Studio open call, featuring a stem of nodding bell-shaped flowers and a cream rose, both on brown. "It perfectly sums up what I enjoy doing right now: flowers, a subject I find delightful, combined with my signature stylistic approach," she says. And what is that approach, you might ask? Well: "simple, synthetic forms, a limited colour palette, including brown (my favourite colour), a mix of angles and curves and those small paper circles from my hole punch (one of my favourite tools)." Those little dots scatter around the edges like confetti, and she deliberately avoids over-editing the colours or saturation so the original scan's "authentic, handmade quality" can shine through.

As for what she hopes people take away from her work, Julie is refreshingly relaxed about it. "There isn't really a message, other than raising my audience's awareness of the poetry found in simple things," she says. She thinks the people who connect with her work appreciate its materiality and "see themselves reflected in the universal motifs I choose to depict."

Plenty is in the works for Julie, including a personal piece for an upcoming exhibition in Sète, plus fairs and markets in London, Marseille, Milan and Valencia in the coming months. She's also about to start a screen-printed book with the Berlin-based studio Le Raclet. And while we have you, she'd like us to know she's "looking to expand my commission work as much as possible (take note!)", with branding projects and press work at the top of her wishlist. "That would be amazing," she says.

The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian ’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits , the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.

“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”

Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.

Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

French street artist Seth Globepainter has created six murals across the Faroe Islands for We Need Art 2026 , drawing upon the archipelago’s maritime heritage, wildlife and cultural traditions to explore childhood, migration and belonging. Set against dramatic coastal landscapes, working harbours and familiar village architecture, the paintings bring Seth’s distinctive visual language into dialogue with the lives of the people who inhabit these North Atlantic islands.

Through images of children, seabirds and symbolic encounters, the series considers what it means to leave home, to imagine a world beyond it and to preserve the traditions that connect one generation to another.

Puffin: A Meeting Between Two Worlds

In Puffin , painted in Kollafjørður, a young boy wearing traditional Faroese clothing and a puffin mask offers a small sand eel to a puffin wearing a human mask. The figures face one another in an unusual exchange of identities, their shared gesture suggesting an attempt to understand the world from another’s perspective.

The painting takes inspiration from the relationship between humans and nature in the Faroe Islands, where fishing, seabirds and the surrounding waters have long shaped everyday life. Seth approaches that relationship through a reversal of familiar roles, allowing the child to assume the appearance of a bird while the puffin takes on human characteristics.

For the artist, the encounter is concerned with harmony, adaptation and empathy. Rather than portraying people and wildlife as separate inhabitants of the landscape, the exchanged masks suggest the possibility of recognising something of ourselves in another living being.

The mural’s setting reinforces that connection. Painted on a harbour building, with the waters of the fjord and surrounding mountains visible alongside it, the work occupies the environment from which its imagery is drawn. In one photograph, a young child wearing traditional Faroese dress sits beneath the painted figures, creating an unexpected relationship between the artwork and the living culture it represents.

Painted on opposing sections of weathered concrete, the two figures are physically separated by a gap in the structure, transforming the existing architecture into an essential part of their story.

Seth connects the painting to the migration of Faroese people who leave the islands in search of employment and opportunities elsewhere. The departing girl becomes a figure of possibility and separation, while the boy who remains watches a departure he cannot prevent.

The artist also draws upon the relationship between Peter Pan and Wendy in J. M. Barrie’s novel, introducing another interpretation concerned with the loss of innocence and the passage from childhood into adulthood. The girl’s flight carries both the excitement of discovering another world and the sadness of leaving something familiar behind.

Positioned among rocky ground, vegetation and residential buildings, the figures appear almost absorbed into their surroundings. The distance between them, emphasised by the physical break in the concrete, gives the painting a quiet emotional force that might have been lost on an uninterrupted wall.

Miss Fanny Hill: the scandalous story of the first porn novel
Despite the very concept being anathema to English culture, at least in the eyes of all the country’s most powerful institutions, porn is everywhere and pretty much always has been.

Even back when it was a literal crime to possess it, there was a thriving black market trade of pornographic images of all kinds going back so far in time we literally can’t even give an educated guess when it began. However, by the end of the 1740s, the taste for salacious materials had gotten so widespread that two particularly daring men decided to do something that would have sounded like the death knell of art at the time.

In 1748, John Cleland hit rock bottom. He’d spent his young adulthood as a soldier in the employ of the East India Trading Company. His goal of rising through the ranks to work as a merchant for the company itself in Bombay, the city he was stationed in. This collapsed, and he was instead sent back to England penniless. His attempts to rebuild his station ended with him accumulating over £800 of debt (equivalent to nearly £100,000 today), so he was arrested and chucked in a debtors’ prison in Fleet Street.

There, Cleland had the time to work on a manuscript he had started in the previous couple of years. Finishing a first draft and sent the first half of it to any publisher of the time who accepted open submissions. One of which was Ralph Griffiths, who was forward-thinking enough to know that the manuscript would be a massive hit despite one major problem. The novel was called Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure , and even by modern standards, it’s absolutely filthy.

The title really does say it all; the novel essentially consists of the titular character reminiscing about her sexual escapades , yet Griffiths thought he could get away with it for one simple reason. Cleland had written the entire thing without ever mentioning an erogenous zone or sex organ. Yeah, turns out the “Bad Sex in Fiction” award winners at least have historical precedent on their side because the very first attempt at getting away with explicit sex in prose still had phrases popping up like “furious battering ram” and “the nethermouth” and (I’m not making this up) “treasure bags of nature’s sweets.”

Attached was a letter explaining Cleland’s situation. Fittingly enough for a man who doesn’t quite come off as a great intellect of the time, this was a damning mistake. Cleland made it clear he was in dire straits, and so Griffiths made an offer to buy the manuscript for 20 guineas (around £6,000 in today’s money). Cleland immediately said yes, and Griffiths published the book in two halves in 1748 and 1749. It was as close to a mega hit as you could get while still being an underground concern that was highly illegal.

So, you remember how Cleland was jailed for £800 of debt? Which was worth around £100,000 of today’s money? Yeah, Griffiths walked away with a fortune of £10,000 pounds from publishing Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure , a novel that began to be popularly known as Fanny Hill after its lead character. As if Cleland wasn’t apoplectic enough about that, he was released from prison shortly after the release of the book’s second volume. At which point the English government caught wind of this perverse porn book, arrested its publisher and, of course, its author.
All this porn talk might make this sound this sound like an innuendo but it bears saying, some people really don’t get lucky, do they?

Cleland avoided going back to prison by expressing remorse for ever writing it, citing the desperation that came from poverty as the reason for his writing something so perverse. This worked out like gangbusters for him, but not only did he avoid prison, he was given a £100 annual pension by the President of the Privy Council in order for him to put his writing talents to better use. Griffiths avoided prison in a way that even the Coens would scoff at for being too ludicrous.

Moondog: the street music legend of 1950s New York City
It’s a cliché to say that New York City has lost a large chunk of its soul to commerce and modernity, but as the legend that is Moondog shows, clichés are only clichés because they’re true.

In fairness, people in the city’s supposed artistic and spiritual heyday of the 1950s to the 1980s said the same. Except that to them, New York City had lost its soul because of the devastating infrastructural neglect and social decay that meant that pretty much every single alleyway outside of the really ritzy neighbourhoods (and a few in them) could be a clear and present danger. It’s difficult to argue with that, except there is something to be said for the fact that characters like Moondog will almost certainly never be found in the city again.

For 30 years, Moondog was an ever-present fixture on the corner of Sixth Avenue between 53rd and 55th Streets. Nearly every single day he could be found selling pamphlets of his poetry and playing music on custom-built instruments that were, broadly speaking, string instruments with built-in percussion instruments. You could also find him there most nights; so fierce was his desire to maintain his prime street corner that he’d often sleep there.

Which must have made for some bizarre drunken trips home for unsuspecting New Yorkers. One second you’re staggering home still buzzed from that night’s pub crawl, the next you’re tripping over the legs of a sleeping Viking.

Because yeah, Moondog had an aesthetic all of his own. One that began in the early days of his time as a busker, where he paired long robes with a shock of brown hair tumbling down his back. He then changed slightly to avoid accusations that he was pretending to be Jesus, adding Viking horns to a helmet to become something slightly less sacrilegious. One might wonder why he didn’t see the accusations coming. Which leads us to possibly the most astonishing part of his whole story.
He couldn’t see it coming because he couldn’t see it at all.

Moondog, or Louis Hardin to his friends, was doing all this while blind. This came from his childhood in his birthplace of Marysville, Kansas, when he picked up an object he found in a field that he didn’t realise was an explosive charge. It detonated in his hands, rendering him permanently blind. However, even before then, he’d established himself as a musical prodigy and, after doing some sundry studies of music theory, decided to work things out for himself, moving to New York to pursue a career as a composer in the 1930s.

After a decade, Hardin’s work was proving too out there and experimental for the classical music gatekeepers at the time, no matter how many famous fans and friends Hardin made at the time. Thus, he decided to devote his time to performing instead. That’s quite literal as well, rather than book gigs, Hardin instead took the name “Moondog” (apparently since he would howl at the moon as a child), and took to his corner of Sixth Avenue, giving his music directly to the people.

Most of the time, he avoided police attention due to the fact that he wasn’t begging. He would only accept money in exchange for a pamphlet of his poetry or, later in life, a recording of his music. He also wasn’t homeless. He’d kept the apartment on 44th Street he bought when he first moved to New York City. Most of all, he wasn’t a figure of pity. Yes, he was an eccentric, but he was also a musical genius who attracted the attention and appreciation of everyone from Leonard Bernstein, Igor Stravinsky, and Charlie Parker.

After 30 years, age finally caught up to Moondog, and his watch on Sixth Avenue finally ended. However, it ended on his own terms. By then, he’d become enough of a cult hero to be known the world over, and was invited to tour Germany. That tour was such a success that he fell for the country, upping sticks and living the rest of his life composing symphonies and occasionally touring Europe, before passing away in 1999.
All hail Moondog. May someday we see his likes again.
‘Tales from the Darkside’ and ‘Amazing Stories’ Thanksgiving Horror TV Episodes Prove the Holiday Deserves…
The reasons why horror generally overlooks Thanksgiving would require a longer discussion, but the fact of the matter is that the day in November for feasts and togetherness has simply…

The reasons why horror generally overlooks Thanksgiving would require a longer discussion , but the fact of the matter is that the day in November for feasts and togetherness has simply never been a popular backdrop in the genre. As scarcely seen as the holiday is in horror movies, it may be even more so in horror television. With that said, we have at least two classic anthology series that don’t omit Thanksgiving from their fantastical offerings. These certain episodes of Tales from the Darkside and Amazing Stories make a case for Thanksgiving being a missed opportunity for holiday terror.

Tales from the Darkside ’s sole Thanksgiving episode, “ The Last Car ”, didn’t air until February of 1986. Syndicated shows weren’t always too concerned with seasonableness, I imagine. The date, however, has no major bearing on the overall story, one in which time loses all meaning. For once you’ve stepped foot in the last car, there is no returning to normal.

Like many people this time of year, Stacey ( Begoña Plaza ) is going back home for Thanksgiving. What should have been a rewarding break from the stresses of higher learning is really the start of a new chapter in her life. The final one, you might even say. As the trip drags on, and the train never seems to reach its destination, Stacey suspects something is amiss.

While watching Tales from the Darkside , you are more likely to find black humor and silliness than sincere scares. “The Last Car”, on the other hand, is distinctively bleak and unnerving from start to finish. Eeriness sets in immediately as Plaza’s character goes from waiting at a desolate train station to entering a small and cold train car occupied by only three other passengers, all of them very strange and cryptic. Anxiety soon follows, complemented by the sheer darkness outside the windows.

Tales from the Darkside was limited by its budget, which led to an extensive array of single-location stories. The same went for the show’s successor, Monsters . Meanwhile, “The Last Car” is an exception, although the bulk of it takes place inside the caboose of an obviously fake train. There is also the matter of the environment ; the space here is more confining than typical venues shown throughout the series. With far less room to walk around in , that sensation of feeling trapped is both instant and unyielding.

“The Last Car” is , arguably , the most that Darkside ever resembled a stage production, and it’s a minimalist one at that. Additionally, director John Strysik shot this episode like an exhibit of sorts . We’re watching the characters move about their enclosed area, seeing how they behave and respond to both each other and that rare external stimulus , namely the train conductor ( Bert Williams ), who changes the protagonist’s round-trip ticket to a one-way. W hile this isn’t exactly a case of a reverse zoo, there is a bit of that quality in the episode’s mise-en-scène . It’s as if the passengers are looking back at us from the not-so-sweet hereafter.

Michael McDowell , the scribe behind Darkside classics like “Halloween Candy” , “Inside the Closet” and “Answer Me”, fared better than other screenwriters in this series; his work was often paired with solid direction. In the case of “Seasons of Belief”, McDowell himself sat in the director’s chair, and fans can agree that it’s one of the show’s best. Yet even under the helm of someone else, his story of purgatory inside of a train car was manifested with good results. The atmosphere and tension make up for any technical shortcomings.

Even though anthologies are known for their twists in the tail , ultimately that’s not what “The Last Car” is after. McDowell, who would soon trifle with death again in Beetlejuice , respects the viewer too much to act as if this whole thing isn’t a giant metaphor for the afterlife. So , yes, this is a fairly straightforward story, but it’s also a haunting one . Instead of fixating on how things are going to end, you can just sit back and enjoy the ride.
Steven Spielberg ’s Amazing Stories dabbled in all genres, which would explain why episodes like Todd Holland ’s “ Thanksgiving ” (1986) can’t be easily categorized . After all, it’s got drama…

You had to know that Rockstar had more than just a “Dexter” reference in store for players in Grand Theft Auto VI .
