YouTuber Punish has documented these newly-discovered Easter Eggs on their channel, kicking off with a chance encounter with a ghostly woman figure that appeared under a streetlight while they were driving around at night (naturally). Your character will react accordingly before your car stalls, and you have a creepy figure rapidly crawl up to your car and start crawling on it.

If you fancy a little occult ritual in your GTA , then head on over to Capri (near the start of the game) and enter an abandoned warehouse across from a railway. From there, you’ll find a pentagram drawn on the floor surrounded by candles. There’s also a table that has a journal on it that looks like something out of The Evil Dead . To activate the ritual, you’ll need to place a body (dead or alive) in the circle. Once that’s done, you’ll have a voice calling out to you from upstairs. Investigate, and lo and behold, you’ve got something resembling Deadite action. Since you don’t have a chainsaw, you’ll end up using a Molotov to send the dead back from where they came.

Grand Theft Auto has dabbled in extraterrestrials before, and it continues here. This is a lengthy one, and it starts off with a UFO abduction in Kelly County. To get that started, head to a road by yourself northwest of the Starlet Motel (east of Port Gellhorn) in Kelly County after 2:00 AM. You’ll find a vehicle with flashing lights. Head up the trail towards the glowing lights. You’ll find a woman who appears to be in the process of being abducted. After “rescuing” her, she asks you to go get her car. Doing so will have you get abducted instead. You’ll wake up three days later, and get an achievement in the process.

After the abduction, you need to keep going to bed with the abducted character until you have a flashback of your abduction, which hints at a location in Leonida. After your dream, head to South Point Airfield, where you can break through the fence and climb onto the roof of the main building to find a hatch. From there, you’ll find a control room, and a live alien in bed. Pick it up and bring it outside. You’ll get a nice reward for your efforts.

This Easter Egg involves you exploring Hyde Island, where you can get darted in the neck and pass out. You’ll awaken in a locked shipping container without any of your gear, but you’ll have a strange collar around your neck. It turns out that you’re being watched by a mysterious figure via a video feed, who seems like a cross between Jigsaw and The Director from Manhunt . They tell you that any attempt to leave the island will have your head leaving your body. After rambling on about how humans have forgotten how to survive as a species, and the need for natural selection to make a comeback, the shipping container is unlocked, and you’ll find yourself being hunted in a kill-or-be-killed situation.

Luckily, there’s a pistol and two bullets nearby. If you manage to dispatch the hunter (and his dog), you’ll earn yourself the hunter’s unique gun. After which, you’ll be sent to the boathouse on the western part of the island. You’ll be able to grab you gear and drive away, with $30,000 in your pocket.

Another Easter Egg (courtesy of IGN) is another less-than-subtle nod to Silent Hill . Players will come across in the form of the Marbelle Hotel in the south area of Crosstown. Entering through the back of the hotel will lead you to a locked safe. Heading upstairs will cause the fun to begin for this one, as the door to the upstairs will open by itself. Entering the room, the lights will go out, and you’ll see strange symbols covering the ceiling and walls, complete with disembodied whispers.
The Crying Boy: how a series of paintings became a tabloid panic

Whether it’s a work of art , a family heirloom or even your laptop, wondering what you’d save from your house in the event of a fire is a common thought experiment for a good reason, but there’s just one problem with it. Fire really doesn’t give you any choice in the matter. They choose what they want to leave, and for one family in 1985, it chose The Crying Boy .

Which sounds like a hopeful, lucky escape on paper but was much less positive than that. The Crying Boy wasn’t a family member, though Ron and May Hall, the married couple who owned the South Yorkshire house which was lost to the fire, both made it out alive. Everything else they had ever called their own was lost, though, save for a painting. Not even a very good one either. A mildly unsettling print of a crying child looking at the viewer. Better than nothing, I guess.

Perhaps that’s why the Halls took this story to The Sun . They needed something to get back on their feet after losing quite literally everything they had, and in the absence of anything else, they had this piece of tat to work with. Their story was that the painting was cursed, and some paranormal entity within it had not only caused the fire, but survived it. What’s more, so they said, the fireman who had put the blaze out had taken one look at the painting and mentioned that there were a number of other paintings just like it.
This wasn’t because he was a fan though, in fact quite the opposite. He knew the series because they had all survived catastrophic fires too.

As you can imagine, The Sun approached this story with healthy scepticism and reservation. Which is to say that the headline of the piece wailed, “Blazing Curse of the Crying Boy Picture!” and spoke of how the artist responsible for these paintings, Giovanni Bragolin, had supposedly painted a series of portraits of a group of orphans left homeless after their orphanage burnt down. Their spirits haunting them for the century to come.

Which sounds like typical tabloid hokum, right? Which is almost certainly what it was… Except the very next month, another house burnt down in Rotherham. The family lost everything save for, you guessed it, another portrait in The Crying Boy series. This went straight into The Sun again, who this time recommended organising a grand burning of all pictures in the series. Again, a little much, but there was at the very least a pattern to follow here.

This sent several investigators down several rabbit holes to decode what this “curse” was all about. Several people couldn’t help but join in with the glorious supernatural nonsense. There were writers claiming that Bragolin, a pseudonym for the Spanish artist Bruno Amarillo, had begun the series by painting a boy named Don Bonillo. The boy had supposedly started a fire that killed his parents. One that he swore was a mistake, but the fact that similarly catastrophic fires followed him wherever he went gave him the nickname Diablo.

Could the paintings carry the spirit of Diablo within them? Sating his untrammelled thirst for fire long after he’s shuffled off the mortal coil? No. Because someone thought to actually look at the paintings that survived the fires and discovered that they, obviously, weren’t paintings. They were printings available in all good British department stores across the 1970s. Y’know, the time and location where aesthetic taste peaked and everywhere else in the world is just playing catch up.

In 2010, British writer and comedian Steve Punt investigated the claims on his BBC Radio 4 show Punt P.I . He examined the prints and found that the varnish used to make them was flame retardant. Y’know what wasn’t? The string used to hold them up. When the heat burnt through the string, the painting would fall face down on the floor and most likely survive even the fiercest of fires.

You can tell this because several prints made by the company that produced The Crying Boy series also tended to survive fires that otherwise totalled people’s lives. However, since there was no spooky child on the front, there was no way for the tabloids to make a fuss about it.

American Nightmare: How a $14,000,000 Ponzi scheme led to two brutal murders
If you're going to turn to crime, at least be good at it.

Unlike more shocking crimes like murders or assaults, the line between con artistry and business sense is wafer-thin at the best of times. Often, the only difference between a bad deal is a crime is who’s on the receiving end of it. If you can afford the court time, you’re golden. If not? Well, it’s your own fault.

However, Joe Hunt wasn’t the kind of person who saw much as his own fault. He was a scholarship kid at an absurdly posh private school in Southern California and, after failing at starting a career as a trader in Chicago, he ended up back in Southern California penniless and with a colossal chip on his shoulder. He decided to take out his anger on the same aimless rich boys he’d gone to school with who were drifting through life on a trust fund, desperate for the validation of their uber-successful families.

Thus, he started a project called The Billionaire Boys Club, a decadent Ponzi scheme where his friends would “invest” in his supposed stock market wizardry, which he’d then use to pay everyone back tenfold. For a while, the scheme was successful. Hunt had built this facade of a ludicrously successful playboy that threw lavish, raucous parties that attracted new “investors”. For a while, Hunt lived the life he always wanted of a 1 per cent-er, the envy of all who saw him.

The problem was that Hunt was still hopeless at manipulating the market, so within months he was not just broke, but deeply in debt. New investors were still coming in though, so he had a few more months of leeway before people started plotting the murders of Hunt and anyone involved in the scheme. This was when Hunt was approached by Ron Levin, a businessman who watched the Club from the sidelines and knew someone desperate when he saw them.

He could tell that under the facade, Hunt was in desperate need of help, so Levin offered him a lifeline. A $5 million trading account he could do with what he wanted, so long as Levin kept half the profits for himself. This time, the strangest thing happened. Hunt finally started hitting it big with this account, and within months, he’d grown the account to $14 million. Finally, he’d achieved wealth on (sort of) his own terms, and thus, he went to the bank to transfer those funds into his own account and get on with spreading the wealth to his Billionaire Boys Club chums.
Except there wasn’t any. The account didn’t exist. Ron Levin knew someone desperate when he saw them because Ron Levin was a conman .

He had faked records of the account Hunt had been “trading” with as documents that helped him secure loans of his own, and now Hunt was well and truly fucked. Desperate and out of ideas, Hunt went to Levin’s Beverly Hills mansion accompanied by the Club’s head of security, Jim Pittman. They forced their way in and made Levin write out a check for $1.5 million at gunpoint. After Levin wrote it out, they shot him dead. I’m sure Hunt never thought there’d be murders in his future when he put the club together, but life’s just mental like that. For Hunt though, it was about to get worse. .

Because the whole thing was moot after all. Levin was a conman, so when Hunt went to cash the check, he found nothing in his bank accounts. Levin was dead and still had Hunt on toast. This was when Hunt confided in his closest circle of Billionaire Boys Club members that he was broke and needed money quickly. After being burned before, Hunt decided to go after the most obvious source of income. The very source of income members of the club had been living off for years. Their fathers.

Madame B: why one of the most forward thinking works of art of the 1800s was a complete mystery

So, turns out the concept behind Pinterest is a lot older than you’d think. This might not be much of a surprise to people aware of the concept of the scrapbook, but it goes back even further than that and well into the art world of the late 1800s.

At the time, it was fairly commonplace for people, mainly upper-class women, to put together large, leather-bound books where they’d paste pictures and photographs of things they found in the press or in a magazine. It wasn’t long until these photobooks evolved into another practice known as the photocollage. These were cases where not only would people paste a photo they liked into these books, but then they’d get to work on painting a picture around them, making a genuine work of recontextualised art.

As you can imagine, the vast majority of these pieces were nothing more than keepsakes. Lovely ones, for sure, but things that people would have likely not taken all that seriously in the stuffy, male-dominated art world of England in the 1800s. There was one exception, though. One that was discovered in France and went from private collection to private collection from the 1800s until 2005, when one of the curators of The Art Institute of Chicago stumbled across it at an antiquarian bookseller’s shop in Tours, France.

This was no keepsake. This was no work of folly to store images the owner liked. This was a trove of simply astonishing multi-media art where every page depicted another breathtaking mix of artful photocollage and a French Master’s deployment of subtle watercolours. Most beguiling of all was the mystery at its heart. The book had changed hands so many times since the 1800s that there was no existing record of who actually made it.
The only possible clue lay on the very first page, where the owner had painted a wooden door with the letter B embossed on it.

This was treated as a possible signature, but even then, it might not have been the case. Even the geography of the book was confusing. Back then, trends rarely bypassed country borders, especially in the case of the United Kingdom, which is, y’know, an island. Trends in England tended to remain there, and yet this was a book that had spent nearly a century in France. A country not exactly known for being fond of British trends, all things considered.

The museum purchased it, where it lay in their archives for the next four years until curator Elizabeth Siegel made it the centrepiece of their 2009 exhibition Playing with Pictures: The Art of Victorian Photocollage . The exhibition became a surprise hit due not only to the beautiful pictures being exhibited from the book, but the very mystery of it all as well. Thus, the museum began an investigation into who exactly the mysterious Madame B was, one that was broken wide open by one researcher looking deep into the photos used and finding the location of the buildings in them.

As if things weren’t confusing enough, this was an English hobby, mastered by a (presumably) French woman… Who was most likely living in Sweden?! The buildings depicted in the photos were from the Scandi country of the 1860s, so now the hunt was on. Researchers cross-referenced French municipal records with families who would have been travelling between England and Sweden from France and, after months, found the diplomat Hugues-Marie-Henri Fournier.

Fournier travelled for work with his family, calling London and Rome his home, along with Stockholm in the 1860s. By that time, he was married to his second wife. A woman whose friends and family all referred to her as Blanche.
Here’s hoping that the work of Marie-Blanche Hennelle Fournier was as appreciated privately as it was publicly well over a century after her passing, because it truly deserved it.
How football hooligans became known as ‘casuals’ in the 1980s
It makes sense in context, I swear!
There’s another word for football hooligan firms. They’re called cults .

Think about it. A large group of people who are constantly looking for new members. All devoted to a single cause. One that is worth more than any individual life, yet is also completely separate from the actual group itself. Combine that with some chanting, some grooming and some truly stomach-churning acts of violence, and you’ve got something truly dangerous going on. Not just in the sense that they’ll mash your face into a wall outside Upton Park station and stab you in the kidneys, though that is a major part of it.

No, the real danger is more insidious than that. The same danger that all cults present. The danger that the people involved in it will find a community that they won’t get anywhere else. One that is, consciously or unconsciously, trying to separate them from any other connection in their life. One of the few benefits of modern, hyper-commercialised English football is that grounds are safer, more diverse places than they’ve ever been, so now we can actually look back and wonder one important question.
Why the shiny hell were they ever called casuals?!

Because… y’know, the very last thing any of them were doing was casual. Yet still, half the established firms called themselves casuals despite defending their turf and their club with the kind of intense devotion that the 300 Spartans would call “a little single-minded”. So, where did this moniker come from? Well, strangely enough, it didn’t come from the really early days of football hooligan firms. As a matter of fact, it came from the moment when firms became enough of a problem to attract police attention.

Which was something of a problem. You see, I don’t want to blow your mind here, but when football supporters go to a game, they like to show their support with merch . Shocking, I know. When these firms started attracting police attention, at first, they were very easy to find. Y’see that group of terrifying psychopaths roaming Fulham Road looking for any poor soul not wearing Royal Blue? Yeah, the ones in the Chelsea scarves? Turns out, those are the Chelsea Headhunters. Best get the cops on the phone.

So, the firms adapted. Club scarves, badges and Doc Martin boots were out, no matter how effective the latter were at breaking noses. So, what would replace them? Nothing high fashion that would attract attention. Nothing too grotty that would make them unwelcome in places like train stations and pubs. They needed the exact middle ground of smart-casual daywear. It would help if it belonged to brands that weren’t all that common in the UK as well, because brands could carry negative associations. New ones didn’t.

This all came together in the late 1970s and early 1980s, when the expansion of European club football meant that for the highest calibre of English teams trips to the continent were fairly common. Their firms brought back rare, high-end sportswear by brands like Lacoste and Fila that could help their firms go unnoticed by police in a way that other firms couldn’t. When the press cottoned onto this, the bizarre sight of blood-soaked thugs dressed in handmade, ludicrously expensive black polo shirts and matching Adidas trainers made them call this new generation of football hooligans “casuals”.

For the rest of the 1980s, casual culture was the scourge of English football. Thus, when the Premier League was formed in 1992, and the apocalyptic amount of money meant that scrutiny on the league was increased tenfold, hooligan firms started dying a painful death for anyone other than Larpers who still believe that people fear the Villa Hardcore or the Inter-City Firm. However, no one could deny that the look was pretty slick when your shirt wasn’t coated in blood and sweat, and your trainers weren’t studded with strangers teeth.

Thus, today, casual culture is simply fashion. Smart, simple and practical, with low-key colours and high-quality tailoring. The kind seen on the stands today and not in alleyways outside it, hitting a grown man with a hammer for supporting Manchester United.
We don’t need to do that anymore. They’ve been through enough.
It Depends on How I Feel in the Morning

The first time I ever left the country, I went with my church youth group. We flew to the Bahamas for a youth conference, and our hotel sat right on the beach. Every morning, I woke up before everybody else. I would slip out, walk down to the water, and wait.

I had never seen anything like it. The color spreading across the water. The quiet. The warmth hitting my face before the day had a chance to get loud. It gave me a peace I couldn’t explain. It felt like I’d been missing something my whole life and didn’t know it until that moment.
I still chase that feeling. Whenever I travel, I’m up before the sun. Every sunrise feels like another shot at life. Another chance to improve, another chance to say something.
People like to ask me what kind of filmmaker I am. It’s a fair question. It’s just hard to answer.

I’ve written, directed or produced more than 18 documentaries and narrative features. One of my documentaries, about a Detroit high school, won three Emmys. I write poems. I write lyrics. I’m in the middle of creating a musical. My team and I produce vertical microdramas, the short series people watch on their phones one episode at a time. Some people are skeptical about this new format. I embraced the challenge. If that’s where people are watching, I want to be there telling them a story.
So what kind of filmmaker am I? Honestly, it depends on how I feel in the morning.
Right now, though, my heart is with Marcus Belgrave, the subject of my new documentary feature, …And Damn He Could Play: The Marcus Belgrave Story .
I didn’t come to this film as a jazz guy. I grew up in Detroit on ’90s hip hop and R&B. But the more I learned about Marcus, the more one question kept bothering me.
Why don’t more people know his name?

This man played trumpet with Ray Charles. He played in the Motown house band. He could stand on a stage next to anybody in the world and hold his own. And still, plenty of trumpet players with lesser gifts became bigger names.

The answer turned out to be the whole movie. Marcus spent his life pouring into other people. For decades, he taught young musicians in Detroit, brought them onto his bandstand, and showed them what it meant to be an artist. Regina Carter. Kenny Garrett. Geri Allen. James Carter. Robert Hurst. The list goes on. He built people, one student, one story at a time.

We spent about four years making this film, and one moment stays with me. We were in the middle of an interview with David Ritz, talking about where Marcus fits in jazz history. I stopped the interview. I pulled him off to the side, because I felt we could nail down the theme statement of the film. He understood my desire and gave an answer that surpassed my request and really shed light on why Marcus was so great.

When people talk about legacy in music, they usually mean fame. Who sold the most records. Who everybody knows. By that measure, sure, some trumpet players are bigger names. But that’s not an honest assessment. When you measure a legacy by what a person leaves behind in other people, by the careers they launched and the lives they shaped, there is no comparison. Marcus’ legacy isn’t one career. It’s generations of them.
That conversation helped me understand what was important to Marcus. It also made me realize what was important to me as an artist.

Because whatever I make on a given morning, it comes back to the same thing. I want to amplify voices that don’t get heard enough. My city. Our young people. The African diaspora. The form of expression changes, but the mission and focus don’t.

I’m a product of Detroit Public Schools. My love for filmmaking started at Communications and Media Arts High School. Today I’m one of the owners of the Collective Studios in Southfield, and we open our doors to local filmmakers who need a place to tell their stories. That matters to me as much as anything I direct.
There’s a ton of boxes out there for artists. People want to know which one you fit in so they can file you away. I understand that. But I’m not getting in one.
I can make a documentary about the box. I can make the box the villain in a thriller. I can write a song about the box, or a whole musical. I can burn the box and create art…

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying…
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

Take, for example, a friend of mine who throws a massive holiday party every year. It’s a Kardashian-level event, if the Kardashians lived in suburbia and wore Anthropologie. We’re talking well over 100 invitees. The guest list probably needs its own zip code. I usually know maybe 20 of them. Thankfully, though, she sends the invite through Facebook, which means I can see exactly who has RSVP’d. I’m not proud of this, but I check it. Repeatedly. Like a day trader watching a stock. If a good chunk of my people are on the “Going” list, I’m in, and I will even put on real pants. If it’s a sea of strangers and one lady I once nodded at in a parking lot, I suddenly remember I might have a thing that night.

Does the guest list influence my decision? Absolutely. Do I feel guilty about it? Also absolutely. I should want to go for the hostess, shouldn’t I? She’s wonderful. Her party is wonderful. Supporting my friend should be reason enough. Instead, I’m evaluating her guest list like a Google review page.

But before you judge me, admit it: You do this too. Everybody does this. Nobody commits to a party completely blind, and anyone who claims otherwise is either lying or has better self-esteem than I do. The real etiquette question is what to do when the guest list isn’t conveniently posted on the invite. Is it rude to just ask the host, straight up, “So who else is coming?” I have thought about this far more than a grown woman should. Here’s where I landed.
The case for asking the host

Everyone wants to know who’s coming. It’s just human nature. The only difference is whether you ask or quietly stalk the RSVP list like it’s an ex’s Instagram. Asking the host is just the honest version of what we’re all doing anyway.

Going to a party takes real effort: the clothes, the sitter, the drive, the small talk, the dessert you bring that you put on a fancy plate hoping no one will notice you got it from the grocery store . Wanting to know whether you’ll see a friendly face at the party isn’t snobbery—it’s basic risk assessment, and the host is the one person who has the answer.
And sometimes, it’s about more than whether the company is fun. I don’t know about you, but if an ex or an ex-friend might be there, I’d at least like a little warning before I walk in.
The case against asking the host

This question is so awkward. How do you even start that conversation? A party isn’t a menu, and your friend isn’t a waiter. Asking who else is coming can sound like you’re ranking their party, and the host might hear, “I’ll only show up if the cool people do.” Nobody wants to feel like their party is the backup plan.
It can also put the host on the spot. She invited you because she likes you, and now she’s reciting names like a court bailiff while wondering if she’s passing some kind of friendship test.

But the biggest issue is that you risk making the host feel unimportant to you, or at least less important than those other people. Because you are literally telling her that she’s not reason enough for you to attend. Ouch.
The real problem isn’t the question

Yet, as awkward as it feels, asking who’s coming isn’t the rude part. What you do next is. The rude part is the limbo where you check “maybe” (or nothing at all) on the RSVP list and let days or weeks go by while waiting to see who else is coming. Meanwhile, your host is just trying to figure out the head count she needs for food, chairs and her own sanity. Hosts aren’t mind readers, and “I’ll let you know” without ever letting them know is so rude.

If this sounds familiar, you’re not alone. In fact, a 2021 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that only about 2% of conversations ended when both people wanted them to. Well, we have the answer to this awkward situation: an expert-recommended technique that’s a lot easier to pull off than you think. Even better? It’s both polite and final.

To master this graceful way out —and also learn how to avoid becoming the person everyone’s trying to ditch—we turned to Adam Mastroianni, PhD, an experimental psychologist and the lead author of the study; Natalie Bernstein, PsyD, a licensed clinical psychologist; and Sabrina Zohar, a relationship coach and the author of Why Am I Like This? Break Your Relationship Patterns and Create the Life You Want .
Read on for the technique you won’t know how you survived without—and memorize this move before your next get-together.
Why do we feel so paralyzed when we’re trapped in a conversation?

Blame it on good manners. Most of us aren’t at a loss for words; we’re just too busy worrying about the other person. “We want out of the conversation, but we don’t want the other person to feel like we’re rejecting them or dismissing them,” Bernstein explains. “We feel bad, because we’re anticipating that they’re going to be disappointed.” And we really don’t want to interrupt someone while they’re talking or, worse, walk away from them mid-sentence.

Plus, for many of us, especially women, the urge to stay put was drilled in early. “We’re taught to go say hi to everybody, be a good girl, don’t ruffle any feathers,” says Zohar. So we do what she calls self-abandoning: We smile and nod to keep everyone else comfortable, “even though internally we might be struggling.”

Even crazier? The person you’re talking to may feel just as trapped as you do. According to Mastroianni’s research, both people are often being polite at the same time . “Neither person wants to offend the other by bailing on the conversation,” he says. “But both people may mistakenly think the other person wants to keep going, when, in fact, everyone is ready to leave.”

The problem is that there isn’t always a graceful off-ramp. “Conversations are a bit like highways: You can’t just leave whenever you want,” Mastroianni says. “You have to wait for the appropriate exit. And that exit might be a few miles down the road, long after you first felt ready to get off the highway.”

It also doesn’t help that we’re terrible at reading one another. In Mastroianni’s study, participants were asked when they had wanted their conversation to end—and to guess when their partner had wanted it to end. On average, their guesses were off by about nine minutes. That’s a big miss, considering the conversations lasted only about 20 minutes on average. In other words, we can misjudge when the other person is ready to go by nearly half the conversation.
What’s the phrase that will get you out of a conversation politely but definitively?

Luckily, there’s a smart way out of any awkward, uncomfortable or just plain boring conversation. Bernstein calls it the Connect and Close technique, which boils down to being direct and physically following through.
First, you deliver this magical line: “It was really nice to see you—I’m glad we got a chance to catch up. I’m going to go say hello to a few other people.”

At the same time, you pair it with some very specific body language . “You can look across the room, wave to someone or shift and turn your body a little bit away while you’re saying it,” Bernstein says. “Then they’re getting information not only from your words but also from what they’re seeing.”

According to the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CSPC), hospital emergency rooms saw nearly 270,000 toy-related injuries in 2025, and 68% of them involved kids under 14. How did the report determine the most dangerous toys of the year?

W.A.T.C.H. does not publish its methodology for choosing the most dangerous toys of the year, but the director of the nonprofit organization, consumer advocate James A. Swartz, has explained the approach in the past.

“We shop for toys, the same way parents and caregivers do, to survey the marketplace,” Swartz told Fast Company in 2019. “The 10 Worst List provides examples of types of hazards acknowledged by the industry over decades—small parts, choking hazards and other examples of hazards as represented by the nominees on the list.”

The group is not a testing organization, and stresses that its goal is to educate parents and the public on hazards posed by toys. The top 10 “worst” toys are intended to be representative of the hazards commonly found in the market, not serve as an exhaustive list.

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above .

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame ) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes , analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963 ). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows . As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said, expressing his dedication to the ideal of (as no less an American auteur than Jerry Lewis described himself) the total filmmaker.

That Kurosawa understood how to tell a story in a way that transcends cultural boundaries goes without saying; what’s less widely appreciated is the way he did so with a combination of simplicity and complexity. As he put it, “a truly good movie is interesting and easy to understand,” two qualities that often end up in irresolvable tension, at least in the hands of lesser filmmakers. Even among those influenced by Kurosawa, for example, some have mastered immediate visual legibility without ever understanding that sound and music are more effectively used as a counterpoint to, rather than mere intensification of, a scene’s prevailing emotion. How many living directors, for that matter, convincingly approach grand, universal themes without irony or protective distance? If Kurosawa’s films retain a power that seems inaccessible today, it may be because, for him, there was no East or West: there was only cinema.

A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)

“ La ciudad es más que la gente. ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión , the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares . Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges ) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones , it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague , political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión , there is no one answer.

One resource can be found at Wiktenauer , a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Battle”) —an Italian fencing manual by Fiore de’i Liberi dating from circa 1404—offers richly- and copiously-illustrated demonstrations of medieval Italian longsword fighting techniques. In the original manuscript, seen here and at The Getty , “the illustrations are inked sketches with gold leafing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wiktenauer entry. Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.
The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere . But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft , managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged : “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker , “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

Though uneasy in the role of movement leader, the author of Anna Karenina invited such treatment by publishing dozens of philosophical and theological works, many of them in opposition to a contrary strain of religious and moral ideas developing in the late nineteenth century. Often called “ muscular Christianity ,” this trend responded to what many Victorians thought of as a crisis of masculinity by emphasizing sports and warrior ideals and railing against the “feminization” of the culture.

Tolstoy might be said to represent a “vegetable Christianity”—seeking harmony with nature and turning away from all forms of violence, including the eating of meat. In “ The First Step ,” an 1891 essay on diet and ethical commitment, he characterized the prevailing religious attitude toward food:

I remember how, with pride at his originality, an Evangelical preacher, who was attacking monastic asceticism, once said to me “Ours is not a Christianity of fasting and privations, but of beefsteaks.” Christianity, or virtue in general—and beefsteaks!

While he confessed himself “not horrified by this association,” it is only because “there is no bad odor, no sound, no monstrosity, to which man cannot become so accustomed that he ceases to remark what would strike a man unaccustomed to it.” The killing and eating of animals, Tolstoy came to believe, is a horror to which—like war and serfdom—his culture had grown far too accustomed. Like many an animal rights activist today, Tolstoy conveyed his horror of meat-eating by describing a slaughterhouse in detail, concluding:

[I]f he be really and seriously seeking to live a good life, the first thing from which he will abstain will always be the use of animal food, because, to say nothing of the excitation of the passions caused by such food, its use is simply immoral, as it involves the performance of an act which is contrary to the moral feeling—killing.

[W]e cannot pretend that we do not know this. We are not ostriches, and cannot believe that if we refuse to look at what we do not wish to see, it will not exist.… [Y]oung, kind, undepraved people—especially women and girls—without knowing how it logically follows, feel that virtue is incompatible with beefsteaks, and, as soon as they wish to be good, give up eating flesh.

The idea of vegetarianism of course preceded Tolstoy by hundreds of years of Hindu and Buddhist practice. East Germany exiled singer Wolf Biermann. They only made his message louder
Fifty years ago the GDR withdrew the citizenship of the prominent leftwing dissident. It turned him into an international symbol – and cemented his place in history

November 16 marks 50 years since one of the most notorious examples of artistic censorship from the 20th century: the East German government’s stripping the citizenship of dissident singer-songwriter Wolf Biermann .
Far from quashing Biermann’s voice, this act of political exile amplified it, and cemented his place in history, underscored by a new documentary about his life story.

It is a lesson others should have done more to heed. Earlier this year, US billionaire Robert Kraft and other stadium owners banned Macklemore from their venues over pro-Palestinian remarks the singer made during his support slot on Ed Sheeran’s tour.
But in trying to silence the rapper, Kraft and his cohort unintentionally amplified his message .
The story of Biermann can tell us much about how attempts to quash the political expression of musicians have spectacularly backfired.
From East German darling to dissident
Biermann, born in 1936, became a prominent figure within East German left-wing dissident artists and intellectuals in the late 1960s. But he wasn’t always an outsider.

As the West German immigrant son of a Jewish communist killed in Auschwitz, and a mentee of Bertolt Brecht, Biermann was initially the darling of the East German press, and held a candidate membership of the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

When his lyrics became critical of the SED, however, the Stasi (secret police) began a campaign of harassment that escalated over more than a decade. It included performance bans, sabotage, intimidation, round-the-clock surveillance, bugging, reports from more than 200 Stasi informants , and even a veiled death threat.
Yet this persecution amplified Biermann’s voice and gave him an international platform.
The making of an international symbol
Western governments adopted Biermann as a potent symbol in the cultural Cold War. He acquired famous fans, including Joan Baez and Allen Ginsberg.
Numerous organisations awarded him prizes. CBS gave him a record deal, and West Berlin radio stations frequently broadcast his music into East Germany.

These broadcasts made some remarkable converts. Gerulf Pannach, a young songwriter and then Stasi informant , first heard Biermann’s music while working as a border guard. He befriended the singer, renounced the Stasi and began writing his own critical lyrics.
Pannach convinced Christian Kunert, the keyboardist of the beloved rock band Renft , to take an anti-state position in 1974.

Kunert, in turn, introduced writer and social psychologist Jürgen Fuchs – who would go on to become a prominent East German dissident – to Pannach and Biermann. He also converted his Renft band mate Thomas “Monster” Schoppe to the cause.
Closer to home, Biermann’s former stepdaughter, young rock singer and future queen of punk Nina Hagen , introduced her bandmates to Biermann.

Biermann’s inner circle was, for a time, paradoxically protected by their fame as dissidents. Aided by Western media, they flouted state controls in ways average East Germans wouldn’t dare. While the state maintained tight surveillance of Biermann’s circle, they seemed hesitant to arrest them.
But those more loosely associated with Biermann often found themselves caught in the crossfire of multiple Stasi operations to harass and crush dissidents.
This included band members of Renft, who helped Pannach bypass his performance ban and perform Biermann’s songs, and publicly denounced East German border policy.
As a result, members of Renft were repeatedly summoned and questioned by the authorities. Then the band was banned. In September 1975, a local licensing board told Renft they “no longer exist”.
Taboo themes in Pannach’s lyrics were the pretext for the ban , but declassified Stasi documents suggest the state ultimately targeted them as proxies for Biermann.
The regime accidentally elevated a popular East German rock band to anti-state legends.

A further attempt to neutralise Renft through conscription and a tax investigation converted the band’s thus far apolitical founder, Klaus Jentzsch, into a gifted anti-state organiser. With Biermann’s help, he coordinated a transnational multi-media campaign.

Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today . “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

“As contemporary students of the Corpus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic principle of Roman law that animals could not be culpable,” Lee adds. “Lacking reason, they were incapable of harboring criminal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman northern France, “the administration of secular justice was still largely the concern of local seigneurs and was governed predominantly by custom rather than statute.” Thus sustained, animal trials served purposes beyond simple punishment. “For medieval people, the world was created by God in a very logical way, with animals created first, in order to serve and help human beings who were created in the image of God,” says University of Liverpool medieval European monster expert Damian Kempf, quoted in Popular Science by Anne Ewbank . In that worldview, trying and executing a pig could “restore what was broken.”

Unlike domestic animals, according to Sonya Vatomsky at JSTOR Daily , destructive mice, beetles, snails, weevils, and other vermin would be sent to ecclesiastical tribunals. “Despite being unlikely candidates for Catholicism, such creatures were punished with excommunication, not execution,” she writes, since casting them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exterminate them with peace of mind. Vatomsky also quotes economist Peter T. Leeson’s theory that the Catholic Church tried more animals when people got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bolstering citizens’ belief in the validity of Church punishments for tithe evasion.” Putting animals on trial may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seeming episode of history, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past society operated — a mode of analysis that gets one wondering how far the modern United States is from giving them the right to sue.
